nameStory: The red-shouldered hawk gets its name from the distinctive rusty-red patches on its shoulders that are visible when the bird is perched. These bright shoulder patches, technically called coverts, catch the eye even from a distance and make this hawk stand out from its relatives.
description: The red-shouldered hawk is a medium-sized hawk with a stocky build and broad wings perfect for soaring through forest canopies. Adults have striking reddish-brown shoulders and underparts with black and white barred wings and tail. They're smaller than red-tailed hawks but larger than sharp-shinned hawks, with a distinctive loud, repetitive call that echoes through wooded areas.

idTips.label: Red shoulder patches
idTips.description: Rusty-red shoulder patches visible when perched, creating a warm chestnut color that stands out against the darker back feathers

idTips.label: Barred wings and tail
idTips.description: Bold black and white bands across the wings and tail, especially noticeable in flight as alternating light and dark stripes

idTips.label: Distinctive call
idTips.description: Loud, repetitive 'kee-yah' call that sounds almost like a blue jay but deeper and more resonant, often heard before the bird is seen

idTips.label: Forest flight pattern
idTips.description: Flies with several quick wingbeats followed by a glide, navigating skillfully between trees rather than soaring high in open areas

idTips.label: Reddish underparts
idTips.description: Breast and belly show warm reddish-brown coloring with fine barring, giving a rusty appearance when viewed from below

habitat: Red-shouldered hawks prefer mature deciduous and mixed forests with tall trees near water sources like swamps, wooded streams, and pond edges. They thrive in areas where forest meets wetland, hunting from perches along woodland borders and flying through relatively open understories beneath the canopy.

seasonality.spring: Most active and vocal during breeding season, with frequent calling and spectacular courtship flights above the forest canopy. Northern birds return from migration and begin nest-building.
seasonality.summer: Adults are busy feeding young and may be seen carrying snakes, frogs, and small mammals to nest sites. Juveniles start appearing with streaky brown plumage lacking the distinctive red shoulders.
seasonality.fall: Northern populations begin migrating south, while year-round residents become less vocal. Juvenile birds are most common and can be confusing to identify without adult coloring.
seasonality.winter: Year-round residents remain active but quieter, often seen hunting along unfrozen streams and wetland edges. Their calls become less frequent but are still distinctive.

funFact: Red-shouldered hawks are surprisingly vocal mimics - they've been recorded imitating the calls of blue jays, and blue jays often mimic hawk calls back, creating confusing conversations in the forest where you might hear a 'hawk' that's actually a jay and vice versa!
confusionNotes: Most often confused with red-tailed hawks, but red-shouldered hawks are smaller, have barred (not solid) tails, prefer forests over open areas, and show red on the shoulders rather than just the tail. Memory trick: 'Red-shouldered' means red on the shoulders when perched, while 'red-tailed' means red mainly on the tail.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'red-shouldered' hawk, the shoulder patches can appear more orange or rusty-brown depending on lighting and individual variation. The scientific name 'lineatus' means 'lined,' referring to the distinctive barred pattern on wings and tail that separates it from other buteos.
compareHints: Among buteo hawks in New England, red-shouldered hawks are the forest specialists with the most distinctive barring pattern. Red-tailed hawks prefer open areas and lack the shoulder patches, while broad-winged hawks are smaller with more pointed wings and different tail banding. Red-shouldered hawks are also the most vocal of the group, calling frequently throughout the year.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's buteo hawks, red-tails are the largest and bulkiest, while red-shouldered hawks are more slender with distinctive reddish shoulder patches and prefer wooded areas.
Compared to its buteo relatives, the broad-winged hawk is the most forest-dependent and migratory.
Unlike the year-round resident Red-tailed and Red-shouldered Hawks, Rough-legged Hawks are strictly winter visitors from the Arctic.
Compared to our common Red-tailed and Red-shouldered Hawks, Swainson's Hawks have longer, more pointed wings and are built more for long-distance soaring.
Ferruginous hawks absolutely dwarf their buteo relatives – they're significantly larger than red-tailed hawks with much broader wings and a more massive build.
